\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{4}{The ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture: internal, conceptual and external (view) levels.}
\ans{2}{3}{Physical data independence is the ability to change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema.}
\ans{3}{4}{Statement I describes logical data independence; physical data independence protects the conceptual schema from changes in the internal schema.}
\ans{4}{4}{DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE; DML: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; DCL: GRANT, REVOKE; TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.}
\ans{5}{4}{DELETE and INSERT are DML commands; TRUNCATE is DDL because it deallocates the data pages.}
\ans{6}{4}{The schema is the intension; the data in the database at a particular moment is the instance (extension or state).}
\ans{7}{2}{The schema is the intension; the instance (extension) changes with every update.}
\ans{8}{1}{IMS is hierarchical, IDMS follows the CODASYL network model, and Codd proposed the relational model.}
\ans{9}{4}{Each child record has only one parent; many-to-many relationships need virtual records.}
\ans{10}{2}{This "data about data" is called metadata.}
\ans{11}{3}{All five are classic problems listed by Silberschatz.}
\ans{12}{4}{Application programs are written by application programmers.}
\ans{13}{4}{Components of the query processor and the storage manager.}
\ans{14}{1}{Three-tier architectures are typical of web applications.}
\ans{15}{4}{The client handles presentation, and the database server handles data management.}
\ans{16}{1}{Distributed DBMSs spread data and software over several sites.}
\ans{17}{3}{Elmasri and Navathe's classification of data models.}
\ans{18}{4}{QBE was developed at IBM by Moshe Zloof.}
\ans{19}{1}{Relational algebra is procedural; SQL and relational calculus are declarative.}
\ans{20}{3}{A view is part of the external level and normally stores no data (unless materialized).}
\ans{21}{2}{Metadata describes the data rather than being the data itself.}
\ans{22}{1}{Because the structure is in the catalog, changing it does not require changing the programs.}
\ans{23}{1}{The transaction manager includes concurrency control and recovery.}
\ans{24}{2}{Classification by number of users: single-user versus multiuser systems.}
\ans{25}{1}{Separate per-application files are a feature of traditional file processing.}
\ans{26}{4}{Integrity constraints are enforced by the DBMS to keep data valid.}
\ans{27}{2}{Categories of database users.}
\ans{28}{3}{SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) was developed for System R.}
\ans{29}{3}{TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates whole data pages without logging individual rows, which is why it is fast and usually not undoable.}
\ans{30}{4}{Conceptual (ER) design is DBMS-independent; logical design maps it to the data model of a DBMS, and physical design is DBMS-specific.}
\ans{31}{3}{Requirements, conceptual schema (ER), logical schema, then physical schema.}
\ans{32}{1}{The storage manager includes the authorization and integrity manager, transaction manager, file manager and buffer manager.}
\ans{33}{2}{File-processing systems preceded DBMSs.}
\ans{34}{3}{Relational algebra specifies a sequence of operations; both calculi are declarative.}
\ans{35}{1}{Cursors are used to bridge the mismatch.}
\ans{36}{4}{The network model allows a member record to belong to several set types.}
\ans{37}{1}{Database designers design the database for an application; system designers build the DBMS software itself.}
\ans{38}{1}{Both are standard textbook statements.}
\ans{39}{2}{Relational systems require a schema first, and storage of tables in files is implementation-dependent.}
\end{answers}

Given below are two statements.\\

\end{question}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{2}{Chen notation as used by Elmasri and Navathe.}
\ans{2}{2}{A weak entity has a partial key (discriminator) and total participation in its identifying relationship.}
\ans{3}{2}{The key of the weak entity is the owner's key plus the partial key.}
\ans{4}{3}{The owner is normally a strong entity type (although a weak entity can, in turn, own another weak entity).}
\ans{5}{4}{One table for each entity set and one for R, with primary key (a1, b1).}
\ans{6}{3}{The key of E1 is added as a foreign key to the table of E2, the "many" side.}
\ans{7}{4}{With total participation on both sides, both entity sets and the relationship can be merged into a single table.}
\ans{8}{2}{The multivalued attribute needs its own table with key (k, m).}
\ans{9}{2}{E1, a table for the multivalued attribute a2, and E2 with a1 as a foreign key: 3 tables.}
\ans{10}{1}{Standard attribute types in the ER model.}
\ans{11}{1}{Total participation (existence dependency) means every entity must take part in at least one relationship instance.}
\ans{12}{1}{Unary (recursive), binary and ternary relationships have degrees 1, 2 and 3.}
\ans{13}{3}{Role names distinguish the participations, for example supervisor and supervisee.}
\ans{14}{1}{For example Supplies(Supplier, Part, Project) differs from Can\_\allowbreak{}supply, Uses and Supplies\_\allowbreak{}to taken together.}
\ans{15}{3}{min = 0 means partial participation; min $\geq$ 1 means total participation.}
\ans{16}{3}{Constraints on specialization and generalization in the EER model.}
\ans{17}{1}{They are inverse processes of each other.}
\ans{18}{3}{Attribute and relationship inheritance is the key property of the IS-A hierarchy.}
\ans{19}{2}{A union type (category) is a subclass of a union of distinct superclasses with different keys.}
\ans{20}{2}{For example Owner is a category of Person, Bank and Company.}
\ans{21}{3}{It is used to express relationships among relationships.}
\ans{22}{4}{In 1:N from Department to Employee, a department can have many employees, but each employee works in at most one department.}
\ans{23}{3}{Placing the foreign key on the side with total participation avoids NULLs.}
\ans{24}{3}{This option works best for total, disjoint specializations.}
\ans{25}{1}{Each value of the multivalued attribute becomes a separate tuple.}
\ans{26}{1}{The key is the owner's key plus the partial key, and Eno is also a foreign key.}
\ans{27}{1}{Hence a relationship attribute such as Start\_\allowbreak{}date can be stored with the employee.}
\ans{28}{4}{Derived attributes are drawn as dashed ellipses.}
\ans{29}{4}{Nulls can mean "not applicable" or "unknown".}
\ans{30}{2}{Multiplicities such as 0..* and 1..1 express cardinality and participation.}
\ans{31}{4}{Chen published the ER model in 1976.}
\ans{32}{2}{One relation for each entity type and one for R, whose key combines the three foreign keys.}
\ans{33}{4}{A key may be simple or composite, and an entity type can have several candidate keys (for example Vehicle\_\allowbreak{}id and Registration).}
\ans{34}{1}{A foreign key Manager\_\allowbreak{}id referencing the same table represents the relationship.}
\ans{35}{3}{Basic ER terminology.}
\ans{36}{1}{Both statements are standard results.}
\ans{37}{1}{Rectangles are entity types and ellipses are attributes.}
\ans{38}{2}{The ER model is a conceptual (high-level) model, and it does not express arbitrary functional dependencies.}
\end{answers}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{3}{The number of tuples is 10 $\times$ 20 = 200, and the degree is 3 + 4 = 7.}
\ans{2}{2}{If every tuple has the same B value the result is 10 $\times$ 20; if no B values match it is empty.}
\ans{3}{4}{Each R tuple matches exactly one S tuple, because B is the key of S and referential integrity holds.}
\ans{4}{1}{(1, 2, 5), (2, 3, 6) and (2, 3, 7); (3, 4) has no matching B in s.}
\ans{5}{4}{Left outer join adds (3, 4, NULL); full outer join also adds (NULL, 9, 9).}
\ans{6}{3}{(1, 2) and (2, 3) have matches in s; a semijoin never duplicates r tuples.}
\ans{7}{1}{Division returns the students enrolled in every course of Course: s1 and s3 (s2 lacks c2).}
\ans{8}{4}{($\pi$\_\allowbreak{}A(R) $\times$ S) $-$ R gives the missing combinations; their A values are removed from $\pi$\_\allowbreak{}A(R).}
\ans{9}{3}{Intersection, join and division can be derived from the basic operations.}
\ans{10}{3}{$\sigma$ selects tuples, $\pi$ selects attributes, $\rho$ renames and $\div$ divides.}
\ans{11}{2}{Removing from R the tuples that are not in S leaves exactly R $\cap$ S.}
\ans{12}{4}{At least the larger relation, and at most every tuple of both if there are no duplicates.}
\ans{13}{1}{Union, intersection and difference require union compatibility.}
\ans{14}{3}{The cascade of projections is equivalent to the outermost projection $\pi$\_\allowbreak{}L1(R), not $\pi$\_\allowbreak{}L2(R).}
\ans{15}{3}{Every candidate key is a superkey, but not conversely.}
\ans{16}{4}{Any superset of \{A\}: 2\textsuperscript{4} = 16.}
\ans{17}{2}{Supersets of A: 16; supersets of B: 16; supersets of both A and B: 8; total 16 + 16 $-$ 8 = 24.}
\ans{18}{3}{Supersets of AB: 8; of CD: 8; of ABCD: 2; total 8 + 8 $-$ 2 = 14.}
\ans{19}{3}{The basic relational constraints.}
\ans{20}{4}{Inserting a new referenced tuple cannot leave any foreign key dangling.}
\ans{21}{4}{An insert can violate all four kinds of constraints.}
\ans{22}{1}{SET NULL and SET DEFAULT are alternatives; RESTRICT or NO ACTION rejects the deletion.}
\ans{23}{1}{Rule 1: all information is in tables; Rule 2: every value is reachable by table, primary key and column; Rule 3: nulls; Rule 4: the catalog is itself relational.}
\ans{24}{1}{Rule 11 is distribution independence, and Rule 0 is the foundation rule.}
\ans{25}{3}{Rules 0 to 12 are usually called "Codd's twelve rules".}
\ans{26}{4}{This is Rule 12.}
\ans{27}{3}{A relation is a set of tuples, so duplicates are not allowed (SQL tables, however, are multisets).}
\ans{28}{1}{A relation with 5 columns and 100 rows has degree 5 and cardinality 100.}
\ans{29}{1}{This equivalence is the basis of Codd's notion of relational completeness.}
\ans{30}{2}{t ranges over Employee tuples that satisfy the condition.}
\ans{31}{2}{Safe expressions restrict results to values in the domain of the expression.}
\ans{32}{2}{It returns the A values of tuples in R.}
\ans{33}{2}{DRC variables range over attribute domains, and QBE is based on domain relational calculus.}
\ans{34}{2}{"For all" queries correspond to division (or to $\forall$ in relational calculus).}
\ans{35}{4}{R $-$ S is generally different from S $-$ R.}
\ans{36}{2}{Natural join is an equijoin followed by removal of the duplicate attribute.}
\ans{37}{1}{Selection returns the tuples satisfying c, which may be none or all.}
\ans{38}{3}{Duplicates are removed, so the number of distinct A values ranges from 1 to n.}
\ans{39}{2}{Both are true, but R concerns primary keys; a NULL foreign key is allowed because referential integrity requires a match only for non-null values.}
\ans{40}{2}{Primary keys never allow NULLs, and a relation can have several candidate keys.}
\ans{41}{1}{Left, right and full outer joins differ in which side's unmatched tuples are kept.}
\ans{42}{1}{It corresponds to GROUP BY with aggregate functions in SQL.}
\ans{43}{3}{Codd's 1970 paper "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks".}
\ans{44}{2}{Relational algebra (Codd, 1970), SEQUEL (1974), QBE (1975--77).}
\ans{45}{3}{(1, 2) and (2, 2): the duplicate (1, 2) is removed.}
\ans{46}{2}{Selection must be applied before projecting away Dno.}
\ans{47}{2}{$\rho$ renames relations or attributes (projection removes attributes), and a natural join with no common attributes equals the Cartesian product.}
\end{answers}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{2}{COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores NULLs.}
\ans{2}{1}{AVG ignores NULLs: 220000 / 4 = 55000.}
\ans{3}{1}{CS has 3 rows and EE has 2; ME has only 1.}
\ans{4}{2}{For the two NULL salaries both comparisons are UNKNOWN, so those rows are not returned.}
\ans{5}{4}{40000, 50000 and 60000; BETWEEN is inclusive and NULLs do not qualify.}
\ans{6}{4}{\_\allowbreak{} matches exactly one character, so the second letter must be s.}
\ans{7}{4}{Only Bala (60000); Farhan's NULL salary makes the condition UNKNOWN.}
\ans{8}{2}{Among the four non-null salaries there are C(4, 2) = 6 ordered pairs with E1 higher.}
\ans{9}{4}{For x = 4, "4 NOT IN (1, 2, 2, 3, NULL)" is UNKNOWN because of the NULL, so no row qualifies.}
\ans{10}{3}{UNION removes duplicates, giving 1, 2, 3, NULL, 4; UNION ALL keeps all 5 + 3 rows.}
\ans{11}{2}{COUNT(x) and COUNT(DISTINCT x) ignore NULL.}
\ans{12}{3}{To test for NULL, IS NULL must be used.}
\ans{13}{2}{UNKNOWN OR TRUE is TRUE; UNKNOWN AND FALSE is FALSE; the others are UNKNOWN.}
\ans{14}{2}{FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, then ORDER BY.}
\ans{15}{3}{Aggregate conditions must go in HAVING (or in a subquery).}
\ans{16}{4}{DELETE is DML; TRUNCATE and DROP are DDL.}
\ans{17}{4}{UNIQUE columns may contain NULLs (in most systems, several), while PRIMARY KEY columns may not.}
\ans{18}{2}{> ALL means greater than the maximum of the set (assuming no NULLs).}
\ans{19}{4}{NOT IN is equivalent to <> ALL.}
\ans{20}{2}{Both are true, but R does not explain A; a correlated subquery is re-evaluated because it refers to columns of the outer query.}
\ans{21}{4}{NOT EXISTS is TRUE when the subquery returns no rows.}
\ans{22}{2}{Types of SQL joins.}
\ans{23}{1}{The Cartesian product has 4 $\times$ 4 rows.}
\ans{24}{3}{Updates through a grouped view cannot be mapped unambiguously to base rows.}
\ans{25}{2}{Otherwise a row could "disappear" from the view after being updated through it.}
\ans{26}{3}{Materialized views speed up queries at the cost of maintenance.}
\ans{27}{3}{Triggers follow the event-condition-action (ECA) model.}
\ans{28}{1}{A statement-level trigger fires once per statement, not once per affected row.}
\ans{29}{1}{Both are advantages of stored procedures.}
\ans{30}{2}{Procedures are invoked with CALL and return results through OUT parameters.}
\ans{31}{3}{The input changes the structure of the query so that its condition is always true.}
\ans{32}{3}{With bound parameters, user input is always treated as data, never as SQL code.}
\ans{33}{1}{Precision 5 is the total number of digits, 2 of which follow the decimal point.}
\ans{34}{1}{Both statements are true.}
\ans{35}{3}{RANK leaves a gap after ties; DENSE\_\allowbreak{}RANK does not.}
\ans{36}{1}{ALTER TABLE changes the schema; UPDATE changes data.}
\ans{37}{1}{SQL keeps duplicates by default because duplicate elimination is expensive.}
\ans{38}{2}{ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work done after the savepoint.}
\ans{39}{3}{A cursor is declared, opened, fetched from and closed.}
\ans{40}{1}{220000 / 6 $\approx$ 36667, which differs from AVG(salary) because COUNT(*) includes the NULL rows.}
\ans{41}{3}{COALESCE returns its first non-null argument.}
\ans{42}{4}{The default order is ascending; ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT, so aliases are allowed.}
\ans{43}{2}{A CHECK constraint is evaluated on insert and update.}
\ans{44}{1}{EXCEPT removes duplicates unless EXCEPT ALL is used.}
\ans{45}{4}{The distinct values 1 and NULL remain; set operations treat NULLs as equal to each other.}
\ans{46}{1}{GRANT gives privileges; REVOKE takes them away.}
\ans{47}{1}{For example SELECT e.name FROM EMP AS e.}
\ans{48}{4}{Standard SQL requires each non-aggregated selected column to be in GROUP BY (or functionally dependent on it).}
\ans{49}{4}{An aggregate cannot appear directly in WHERE; a scalar subquery is used instead.}
\ans{50}{2}{They provide call-level interfaces, unlike embedded SQL, which needs a precompiler.}
\ans{51}{3}{SQL tables are multisets; only constraints such as PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE prevent duplicates.}
\end{answers}

\section{Functional Dependencies and Normalization (closure, keys, Armstrong's axioms, minimal cover, 1NF--5NF, decomposition)}

\begin{question}{H}
For the relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = \{A $\rightarrow$ BC, CD $\rightarrow$ E, B $\rightarrow$ D, E $\rightarrow$ A\}, the closure B\textsuperscript{+} is
\optsshort{\{A, B, C, D, E\}}{\{B, C, D\}}{\{B, D\}}{\{B\}}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
For the relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = \{A $\rightarrow$ BC, CD $\rightarrow$ E, B $\rightarrow$ D, E $\rightarrow$ A\}, the candidate keys are
\optsshort{A, B, C and D}{A and E only}{BC and CD only}{A, E, BC and CD}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
For the relation R(A, B, C, G, H, I) with F = \{A $\rightarrow$ B, A $\rightarrow$ C, CG $\rightarrow$ H, CG $\rightarrow$ I, B $\rightarrow$ H\}, the closure (AG)\textsuperscript{+} is
\optsshort{\{A, B, C, G, H, I\}}{\{A, G, H, I\}}{\{A, B, C, G, H\}}{\{A, B, C, G\}}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
Match List I with List II.\\
List I (Armstrong's axiom or inference rule): A. Reflexivity  B. Augmentation  C. Transitivity  D. Pseudotransitivity\\
List II (Rule): I. If X $\rightarrow$ Y and WY $\rightarrow$ Z, then WX $\rightarrow$ Z  II. If X $\rightarrow$ Y and Y $\rightarrow$ Z, then X $\rightarrow$ Z  III. If Y $\subseteq$ X, then X $\rightarrow$ Y  IV. If X $\rightarrow$ Y, then XZ $\rightarrow$ YZ
\optsshort{A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I}{A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I}{A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II}{A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
Given below are two statements.\\
Statement I: Armstrong's axioms are sound: they generate only functional dependencies that actually hold.\\
Statement II: Armstrong's axioms are complete: repeated application generates all dependencies in F\textsuperscript{+}.
\optslong{Both Statement I and Statement II are true}{Both Statement I and Statement II are false}{Statement I is true but Statement II is false}{Statement I is false but Statement II is true}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
Which of the following inference rules is NOT valid for functional dependencies?
\optslong{If X $\rightarrow$ YZ, then X $\rightarrow$ Y}{If X $\rightarrow$ Y and X $\rightarrow$ Z, then X $\rightarrow$ YZ}{If XY $\rightarrow$ Z, then X $\rightarrow$ Z}{If X $\rightarrow$ Y and YW $\rightarrow$ Z, then XW $\rightarrow$ Z}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}

\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}

\optsshort{2NF}{1NF}{3NF}{BCNF}

\begin{question}{H}
The relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with F = \{A $\rightarrow$ B, B $\rightarrow$ C, C $\rightarrow$ D, D $\rightarrow$ A, E $\rightarrow$ F\} has how many candidate keys?
\optsshort{2}{1}{6}{4}

\begin{question}{M}
The relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with F = \{A $\rightarrow$ B, B $\rightarrow$ C, C $\rightarrow$ D, D $\rightarrow$ A, E $\rightarrow$ F\} is in which highest normal form?
\optsshort{BCNF}{1NF}{2NF}{3NF}

\begin{question}{M}
The relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = \{AB $\rightarrow$ C, DE $\rightarrow$ B, C $\rightarrow$ D\} has which candidate keys?
\optsshort{AB only}{AE and BE}{ABE only}{ABE, ACE and ADE}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{M}
The relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = \{AB $\rightarrow$ C, DE $\rightarrow$ B, C $\rightarrow$ D\} is in which highest normal form?
\optsshort{1NF}{2NF}{3NF}{BCNF}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
The relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J) with F = \{AB $\rightarrow$ C, A $\rightarrow$ DE, B $\rightarrow$ F, F $\rightarrow$ GH, D $\rightarrow$ IJ\} has the candidate key
\optsshort{AB}{ABD}{A}{ABF}

\begin{question}{M}
The relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J) with F = \{AB $\rightarrow$ C, BD $\rightarrow$ EF, AD $\rightarrow$ GH, A $\rightarrow$ I, H $\rightarrow$ J\} has the candidate key
\optsshort{BD}{AB}{AD}{ABD}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{M}
The relation R(V, W, X, Y, Z) with F = \{V $\rightarrow$ W, VW $\rightarrow$ X, Y $\rightarrow$ VX, Y $\rightarrow$ Z\} is in which highest normal form?
\optsshort{3NF}{1NF}{2NF}{BCNF}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
Match List I with List II.\\
List I (Normal form): A. 1NF  B. 2NF  C. 3NF  D. BCNF\\
List II (Condition): I. For every non-trivial X $\rightarrow$ Y, X is a superkey  II. Every attribute value is atomic  III. No non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a candidate key  IV. No non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key
\optsshort{A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV}{A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I}{A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I}{A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
A relation R is in 3NF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X $\rightarrow$ A,
\optslong{X is a candidate key and A is non-prime}{X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute}{A is a prime attribute}{X is a superkey}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}

\begin{question}{M}

\optslong{Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A}{Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A}{A is true but R is false}{A is false but R is true}
\end{question}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{3}{B $\rightarrow$ D, and no other dependency has its left side contained in \{B, D\}.}
\ans{2}{4}{A\textsuperscript{+} = ABCDE; E $\rightarrow$ A; BC $\rightarrow$ BCD $\rightarrow$ E; CD $\rightarrow$ E $\rightarrow$ A. No single attribute other than A and E is a key.}
\ans{3}{1}{A gives B and C; CG then gives H and I. So AG is a superkey.}
\ans{4}{2}{Union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity can be derived from the three axioms.}
\ans{5}{1}{Soundness and completeness of Armstrong's axioms.}
\ans{6}{3}{A dependency cannot be weakened on the left: XY $\rightarrow$ Z does not imply X $\rightarrow$ Z.}
\ans{7}{2}{Combine A $\rightarrow$ BC and A $\rightarrow$ B; A is extraneous in AB $\rightarrow$ C; C is extraneous in A $\rightarrow$ BC because A $\rightarrow$ B $\rightarrow$ C.}
\ans{8}{4}{A $\rightarrow$ C and AC $\rightarrow$ D give A $\rightarrow$ CD; E $\rightarrow$ AD and A $\rightarrow$ C give everything in F, and E $\rightarrow$ AH plus A $\rightarrow$ CD gives back E $\rightarrow$ AD.}
\ans{9}{2}{The only key is A (a single attribute), so there are no partial dependencies, but B $\rightarrow$ C is transitive.}
\ans{10}{3}{The key is AB, and B $\rightarrow$ D is a partial dependency of the non-prime attribute D.}
\ans{11}{4}{Keys are AB and BC. C $\rightarrow$ A violates BCNF, but A is prime, so R is in 3NF.}
\ans{12}{4}{Every attribute is a candidate key, so every determinant is a superkey.}
\ans{13}{4}{E must be in every key; AE, BE, CE and DE are the candidate keys.}
\ans{14}{2}{E $\rightarrow$ F is a partial dependency: E is part of every key and F is non-prime.}
\ans{15}{4}{D $\rightarrow$ A: D is not a superkey, but A is prime, so the relation is in 3NF but not BCNF.}
\ans{16}{4}{E and A appear on no right-hand side, so every key contains AE; adding B, C or D gives a key.}
\ans{17}{3}{All attributes are prime (keys ABE, ACE, ADE), so 3NF holds, but C $\rightarrow$ D violates BCNF.}
\ans{18}{1}{(AB)\textsuperscript{+} = ABCDEFGHIJ, and neither A nor B alone determines everything.}
\ans{19}{4}{A, B and D appear on no right-hand side, so they must be in every key, and ABD determines all attributes.}
\ans{20}{3}{The only key is Y, so there is no partial dependency, but V $\rightarrow$ W is transitive.}
\ans{21}{2}{Definitions of the normal forms based on functional dependencies.}
\ans{22}{2}{BCNF drops the second alternative.}
\ans{23}{3}{BCNF is stricter; R(A, B, C) with AB $\rightarrow$ C and C $\rightarrow$ A is in 3NF but not BCNF.}
\ans{24}{1}{In R(A, B), A $\rightarrow$ B makes A a key and B $\rightarrow$ A makes B a key.}
\ans{25}{3}{Partial dependency requires a composite key, so such a relation cannot violate 2NF (it may still violate 3NF).}
\ans{26}{2}{A decomposition into R1 and R2 is lossless if R1 $\cap$ R2 $\rightarrow$ R1 or R1 $\cap$ R2 $\rightarrow$ R2.}
\ans{27}{1}{The common attribute B determines neither AB nor BC, so spurious tuples can appear.}
\ans{28}{1}{A is a key and appears in every relation, so it is lossless, but B $\rightarrow$ C and C $\rightarrow$ D cannot be checked within any single relation.}
\ans{29}{4}{Each dependency lies inside one relation, and the chain of keys joins losslessly.}
\ans{30}{3}{R1 $\cap$ R2 = C $\rightarrow$ A, so it is lossless; but AB $\rightarrow$ C spans both relations.}
\ans{31}{4}{The 3NF synthesis algorithm guarantees both properties; BCNF decomposition is lossless but may lose dependencies.}
\ans{32}{3}{R1 $\cap$ R2 = C, and C\textsuperscript{+} = C, which is not a key of either relation.}
\ans{33}{2}{R1 $\cap$ R2 = A, and A is a key of R1 (indeed of R).}
\ans{34}{4}{Higher normal forms deal with multivalued and join dependencies.}
\ans{35}{2}{Every FD X $\rightarrow$ Y is also an MVD X $\twoheadrightarrow$ Y.}
\ans{36}{3}{MVDs generalise FDs; the converse does not hold.}
\ans{37}{1}{Course $\twoheadrightarrow$ Teacher and Course $\twoheadrightarrow$ Book are non-trivial MVDs whose determinant is not a superkey.}
\ans{38}{4}{MVDs always come in complementary pairs.}
\ans{39}{3}{Normalization generally increases the number of joins; denormalization is sometimes used for performance.}
\ans{40}{1}{It arises when facts about different entities are stored in one relation.}
\ans{41}{4}{1NF is part of the basic definition of a relation.}
\ans{42}{2}{Non-prime attributes are not part of any candidate key.}
\ans{43}{4}{Attribute closure X\textsuperscript{+} is used to test whether X $\rightarrow$ Y is in F\textsuperscript{+}.}
\ans{44}{2}{D $\rightarrow$ A, so BD $\rightarrow$ ABD $\rightarrow$ ABCD; B alone determines nothing, and AD lacks B.}
\ans{45}{4}{AC is the key; A $\rightarrow$ B is a partial dependency of the non-prime attribute B.}
\ans{46}{1}{Both follow from augmentation and union (I is augmentation with reflexivity).}
\ans{47}{4}{Removing extraneous attributes is a step in computing a canonical cover.}
\ans{48}{3}{Trivial dependencies always hold, for example AB $\rightarrow$ A.}
\ans{49}{1}{E and H appear on no right-hand side; EH\textsuperscript{+} = EHC, and adding A, B or D completes a key.}
\ans{50}{2}{2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF and then 5NF; each is stricter than the previous one.}
\ans{51}{4}{This is the binary lossless-join test.}
\ans{52}{1}{Otherwise some dependency can only be checked by joining relations.}
\ans{53}{1}{DKNF was proposed by Fagin as the "ultimate" normal form.}
\ans{54}{4}{Two tuples with the same A value (a1) must have the same B value.}
\ans{55}{3}{Date and Fagin showed that a 3NF relation whose keys are all simple is in BCNF (indeed in 5NF), so A is true; R is false because 3NF also allows X $\rightarrow$ A when A is prime.}
\end{answers}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{2}{p $\times$ 6 + (p $-$ 1) $\times$ 9 $\leq$ 512 gives 15p $\leq$ 521, so p = 34.}
\ans{2}{3}{q $\times$ (9 + 7) + 6 $\leq$ 512 gives 16q $\leq$ 506, so q = 31.}
\ans{3}{4}{6p + 9(p $-$ 1) $\leq$ 1024 gives 15p $\leq$ 1033, so p = 68.}
\ans{4}{3}{8p + 12(p $-$ 1) $\leq$ 4096 gives 20p $\leq$ 4108, so p = 205.}
\ans{5}{2}{bfr = 10 records per block, so 3000 blocks; $\lceil$log2 3000$\rceil$ = 12.}
\ans{6}{2}{68 entries per index block; 3000 entries need 45 blocks; $\lceil$log2 45$\rceil$ = 6 index accesses plus 1 data access.}
\ans{7}{2}{One entry per record: $\lceil$30,000 / 68$\rceil$ = 442 blocks.}
\ans{8}{2}{Level 1 needs $\lceil$3000 / 68$\rceil$ = 45 blocks; level 2 needs 1 block. Search cost is 2 index accesses + 1 data access.}
\ans{9}{2}{A file can have at most one primary or clustering index, but many secondary indexes.}
\ans{10}{1}{Each data block has one anchor record in a primary index; a secondary index must point to every record.}
\ans{11}{1}{Higher fan-out gives fewer levels, and linked leaves support sequential access.}
\ans{12}{3}{B+ tree leaves are linked to support range queries.}
\ans{13}{1}{The root needs at least 2 pointers if it is an internal node.}
\ans{14}{3}{All leaves are at the same depth, which is logarithmic in n.}
\ans{15}{4}{Basic file organizations.}
\ans{16}{3}{If the local depth is less than the global depth, the bucket is split without doubling the directory.}
\ans{17}{4}{The directory has 2\textsuperscript{d} entries, where d is the global depth.}
\ans{18}{4}{Buckets are split in linear order, with overflow chains handling temporary overflow.}
\ans{19}{3}{Too many overflow buckets degrade performance, which motivates dynamic hashing.}
\ans{20}{2}{n\_\allowbreak{}r $\times$ b\_\allowbreak{}s + b\_\allowbreak{}r = 5000 $\times$ 400 + 100 = 2,000,100.}
\ans{21}{3}{b\_\allowbreak{}r $\times$ b\_\allowbreak{}s + b\_\allowbreak{}r = 100 $\times$ 400 + 100 = 40,100 block transfers.}
\ans{22}{2}{Each relation is read only once: b\_\allowbreak{}r + b\_\allowbreak{}s = 500.}
\ans{23}{3}{Each block is read once; if unsorted, sorting cost must be added.}
\ans{24}{3}{The three basic steps of query processing.}
\ans{25}{1}{Pushing selections and projections down reduces the size of intermediate results.}
\ans{26}{1}{Most optimizers combine both approaches.}
\ans{27}{1}{For n = 3 it is 12, and for n = 7 it is 665,280, which is why optimizers use dynamic programming.}
\ans{28}{4}{Sorting and some aggregations are blocking operations that need their whole input before producing output.}
\ans{29}{2}{Selection on a Cartesian product is a theta join; projection does not distribute over difference in general.}
\ans{30}{4}{Optimizers use selectivity to estimate the size of intermediate results.}
\ans{31}{1}{Assuming uniform distribution: n\_\allowbreak{}r / V(A, r) = 10,000 / 50 = 200.}
\ans{32}{2}{Sorted runs are created and then merged in one or more passes.}
\ans{33}{1}{Tuples are partitioned on the hash of the join attribute, so only equality conditions can be used.}
\ans{34}{1}{The query can be answered from the index alone (an index-only scan).}
\ans{35}{4}{Data can be physically ordered in only one way, so there is at most one clustered index.}
\ans{36}{3}{R-trees index multidimensional objects using minimum bounding rectangles.}
\ans{37}{4}{One bit vector per distinct value allows fast Boolean combination of conditions.}
\ans{38}{2}{One access per tree level plus one access to the data block.}
\ans{39}{1}{B+ trees grow at the root, which keeps all leaves at the same depth.}
\ans{40}{4}{n\_\allowbreak{}r is the number of tuples and l\_\allowbreak{}r the size of a tuple.}
\ans{41}{3}{ISAM indexes do not change on updates, so overflow chains grow; B+ trees replaced them.}
\ans{42}{4}{Hashing scatters adjacent key values, so range queries need a full scan.}
\ans{43}{2}{A node with m child pointers holds m $-$ 1 keys.}
\end{answers}

\section{Transaction Processing and Concurrency Control (ACID, schedules, serializability, recoverability, locking, timestamps)}

\begin{question}{H}
Match List I with List II.\\
List I (ACID property): A. Atomicity  B. Consistency  C. Isolation  D. Durability\\
List II (Responsible component or meaning): I. Recovery manager ensures committed changes survive failures  II. Concurrency-control manager makes concurrent execution look serial  III. Transaction is all-or-nothing, ensured by the recovery (undo) mechanism  IV. A correct transaction preserves database integrity constraints; responsibility of the programmer
\optsshort{A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II}{A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I}{A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I}{A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}

A. Committed  B. Active  C. Partially committed

\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}

\end{question}

\end{question}

\optslong{S is serial}{S is not conflict serializable}{S is conflict serializable as T1, T2}{S is conflict serializable as T2, T1}
\end{question}

\optslong{checking that every transaction commits}{checking that the precedence graph is acyclic}{counting the number of locks}{checking that no transaction reads uncommitted data}

Match List I with List II.\\

Rows satisfying a condition appear when the query is re-executed because another transaction inserted them  III. An update by one transaction is overwritten by another  IV. A transaction reads the same item twice and gets different values
\optsshort{A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II}{A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II}{A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II}{A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV}

\begin{question}{H}

\optsshort{A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II}{A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I}{A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I}{A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{2}{ACID properties and the components that enforce them.}
\ans{2}{4}{A failing transaction goes from active or partially committed to failed and then aborted.}
\ans{3}{2}{All conflicting pairs order T1 before T2, so the precedence graph has only the edge T1 $\rightarrow$ T2.}
\ans{4}{3}{r2(A) before w1(A) gives T2 $\rightarrow$ T1, and r1(A) before w2(A) gives T1 $\rightarrow$ T2: a cycle (a lost update). With no blind writes, it is not view serializable either.}
\ans{5}{1}{The precedence graph has a cycle between T1 and T2, but S is view equivalent to T1, T2, T3 because w2(A) and w1(A) are blind writes overwritten by T3.}
\ans{6}{3}{A view-serializable schedule that is not conflict serializable must contain blind writes.}
\ans{7}{4}{Edges: T3 $\rightarrow$ T1 (r3(X) before w1(X)), T1 $\rightarrow$ T2 (r1(Z) before w2(Z)) and T3 $\rightarrow$ T2 (w3(Y) before r2(Y)); the topological order is T3, T1, T2.}
\ans{8}{2}{On X, T1 precedes T2; on Y, T2 precedes T1, giving a cycle.}
\ans{9}{2}{If the precedence graph has no cycle, a topological sort gives an equivalent serial order.}
\ans{10}{1}{Read-read pairs never conflict.}
\ans{11}{2}{C(5, 2) = 10.}
\ans{12}{1}{6! / (2! $\times$ 2! $\times$ 2!) = 90.}
\ans{13}{1}{Any ordering of the n transactions is a serial schedule.}
\ans{14}{4}{Strict $\subseteq$ cascadeless $\subseteq$ recoverable.}
\ans{15}{4}{T2 has committed a value that never officially existed; the DBMS cannot undo T2.}
\ans{16}{1}{If no one reads uncommitted data, aborting one transaction cannot force others to roll back.}
\ans{17}{3}{Classic anomalies of concurrent execution.}
\ans{18}{4}{SQL-92 isolation levels and the phenomena they allow.}
\ans{19}{4}{2PL can deadlock; deadlock handling is needed separately.}
\ans{20}{3}{Serializability order corresponds to the order of the lock points.}
\ans{21}{2}{Both are true, but A holds because strict 2PL keeps exclusive locks until commit or abort, which R does not mention.}
\ans{22}{1}{Under rigorous 2PL, transactions can be serialized in the order in which they commit.}
\ans{23}{3}{If any lock is unavailable, the transaction waits without holding any locks.}
\ans{24}{3}{Several transactions can read an item simultaneously, but a write needs an exclusive lock.}
\ans{25}{2}{Intention locks are used in multiple-granularity locking.}
\ans{26}{3}{IX is compatible with IS and IX; S is compatible only with IS and S.}
\ans{27}{1}{A younger transaction has already read Q, so the value T would write is needed too late.}
\ans{28}{1}{Ignoring the outdated write allows some view-serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.}
\ans{29}{3}{No transaction ever waits, so there is no deadlock; but schedules may be non-recoverable unless extended (for example by delaying commits).}
\ans{30}{1}{In wait-die an older requester waits and a younger requester dies; in wound-wait an older requester wounds the younger holder and a younger requester waits.}
\ans{31}{1}{Keeping the original timestamp ensures it eventually becomes the oldest, preventing starvation.}
\ans{32}{3}{Transactions work on local copies, validate, then write if validation succeeds.}
\ans{33}{4}{Optimistic methods use no locks; they check for conflicts at validation time.}
\ans{34}{4}{A read returns the appropriate older version; writes may still cause rollbacks.}
\ans{35}{3}{Two transactions reading overlapping data and writing disjoint items can violate a constraint.}
\ans{36}{4}{Locks on the index ranges or predicates also cover tuples that do not yet exist.}
\ans{37}{1}{The tree protocol is deadlock-free and allows earlier unlocking than 2PL.}
\ans{38}{1}{The lock manager must grant requests fairly to avoid it.}
\ans{39}{3}{A cycle in the wait-for graph indicates a deadlock; a victim is then rolled back.}
\ans{40}{4}{r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 $\rightarrow$ T2, and w2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 $\rightarrow$ T1, so there is a cycle.}
\ans{41}{1}{Every serial schedule is serializable.}
\ans{42}{1}{Conflict serializability needs only a cycle check on the precedence graph.}
\ans{43}{1}{A hardware failure at this point could still prevent its successful completion.}
\ans{44}{2}{After unlock(A) begins the shrinking phase, no new lock can be acquired.}
\ans{45}{1}{Downgrades are allowed only in the shrinking phase.}
\ans{46}{3}{It maintains a lock table, often a hash table keyed by data item.}
\end{answers}

\section{Database Recovery, Security and Authorization}

\begin{question}{H}
Match List I with List II.\\
List I (Recovery technique): A. Deferred update  B. Immediate update  C. Shadow paging\\
List II (Operations needed after a crash): I. NO-UNDO/NO-REDO  II. NO-UNDO/REDO  III. UNDO/REDO
\optsshort{A-II, B-I, C-III}{A-II, B-III, C-I}{A-I, B-III, C-II}{A-III, B-II, C-I}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
The write-ahead logging (WAL) rule requires that
\optslong{log records be written only at commit}{the log records for an update be written to stable storage before the updated data page is written to disk}{the log be deleted after each checkpoint}{data pages be written before log records}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
A log contains, in order: <T1 start>, <T1, A, 10, 20>, <T2 start>, <T1 commit>, <checkpoint \{T2\}>, <T3 start>, <T2, B, 5, 15>, <T3, C, 7, 9>, <T3 commit>, and then the system crashes. With immediate update, the recovery manager must
\optsshort{undo T3 and redo T2}{undo T2 and redo T3}{undo T1 and T2}{redo T1, T2 and T3}
\end{question}

\begin{question}{H}
Given below are two statements.\\
Statement I: A checkpoint reduces the amount of the log that must be scanned during recovery.\\
Statement II: Transactions that committed before the last checkpoint must be redone after a crash.

\begin{question}{H}

\begin{question}{M}
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.\\
Assertion A: Log records must be written to stable storage before the transaction's commit record is considered complete.\\
Reason R: Otherwise a committed transaction's updates could be lost in a crash, violating durability.
\optslong{Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A}{Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A}{A is true but R is false}{A is false but R is true}
\end{question}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{2}{Deferred update writes nothing to the database before commit; shadow paging switches page tables atomically at commit.}
\ans{2}{2}{Also, all log records of a transaction must be forced before it commits.}
\ans{3}{2}{T1 committed before the checkpoint, so its updates are already on disk; T3 committed after it and must be redone; T2 never committed and must be undone.}
\ans{4}{3}{Their changes were flushed to disk at the checkpoint, so they need neither undo nor redo.}
\ans{5}{3}{Most real systems use steal/no-force, which requires both UNDO and REDO.}
\ans{6}{3}{Analysis finds dirty pages and active transactions; redo repeats history; undo rolls back losers.}
\ans{7}{1}{CLRs are redo-only records that make undo idempotent across repeated crashes.}
\ans{8}{2}{The old value is used for undo and the new value for redo.}
\ans{9}{3}{Updated pages change location on disk, which destroys clustering.}
\ans{10}{4}{Media failure requires restoring from a backup and replaying the archived log.}
\ans{11}{4}{Because of R, uncommitted transactions never changed the database, so no UNDO is needed.}
\ans{12}{3}{The log is kept on stable storage.}
\ans{13}{1}{A crash during recovery may cause the same redo to be repeated.}
\ans{14}{4}{Revoking with CASCADE then also removes the privileges the recipient granted.}
\ans{15}{2}{C's privilege depended on B's grant, so it is removed when B's is.}
\ans{16}{1}{DAC, MAC and RBAC.}
\ans{17}{2}{"No read up" and "no write down" prevent information flowing to lower classes.}
\ans{18}{3}{Users can be given access to a view without any privilege on the underlying tables.}
\ans{19}{4}{Countermeasures include minimum query-set sizes and adding noise.}
\ans{20}{4}{It prevents low-clearance users from inferring the existence of high-classification data.}
\ans{21}{1}{The general form is GRANT privileges ON object TO users [WITH GRANT OPTION].}
\ans{22}{3}{Authorised users with the key can still query the data; R is false.}
\ans{23}{2}{Auditing helps detect misuse and is required by many regulations.}
\ans{24}{4}{Other methods include partitioning the database and perturbing results.}
\ans{25}{2}{Roles simplify the administration of privileges.}
\ans{26}{1}{Losers are undone; winners are redone (subject to checkpoints).}
\ans{27}{3}{T1 did not commit, so it is undone using the old values, in reverse order.}
\ans{28}{4}{A fuzzy checkpoint lets transactions continue while dirty pages are written.}
\ans{29}{4}{A poor plan is a performance problem, not a failure needing recovery.}
\ans{30}{1}{If the primary fails, the backup takes over.}
\ans{31}{2}{Any language that builds SQL strings from input is vulnerable, and prepared statements are the primary defence.}
\ans{32}{4}{CASCADE removes dependent privileges as well.}
\ans{33}{1}{The creator (owner) of an object holds every privilege on it.}
\ans{34}{1}{This is the commit rule of write-ahead logging.}
\end{answers}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{3}{Enhanced data models covered in Elmasri and Navathe.}
\ans{2}{1}{A bitemporal database records both valid time and transaction time.}
\ans{3}{2}{Valid-time-only databases are historical; transaction-time-only databases are rollback databases.}
\ans{4}{3}{The head is derived when all literals in the body are true; facts are rules with empty bodies.}
\ans{5}{1}{Recursive views in SQL:1999 (WITH RECURSIVE) offer similar power.}
\ans{6}{1}{Stratified negation gives a well-defined meaning to programs with negation.}
\ans{7}{4}{XML schema and query standards from the W3C.}
\ans{8}{1}{It is analogous to SELECT-FROM-WHERE in SQL.}
\ans{9}{3}{A valid document must also conform to its DTD or schema; well-formedness alone is not enough.}
\ans{10}{2}{XML is self-describing, with tags giving structure but no fixed schema required.}
\ans{11}{2}{Basic concepts of object-oriented databases.}
\ans{12}{1}{ODL is the Object Definition Language and OQL the Object Query Language.}
\ans{13}{1}{Both statements are true.}
\ans{14}{2}{Value-based identity (keys) is the relational approach.}
\ans{15}{3}{Object databases store objects with the type system of the programming language, which is why the mismatch is reduced.}
\ans{16}{2}{A set has no duplicates; lists and arrays are ordered.}
\ans{17}{3}{Horizontal fragments are reconstructed by union, vertical fragments by join.}
\ans{18}{2}{It is the other way round: horizontal fragments are combined by union and vertical fragments by join.}
\ans{19}{2}{Types of distribution transparency.}
\ans{20}{3}{Phase 1 is voting (prepare and votes); phase 2 is the decision (commit or abort).}
\ans{21}{1}{Three-phase commit was proposed to reduce this blocking.}
\ans{22}{1}{Commit requires unanimous "ready" votes.}
\ans{23}{3}{Only the tuples that will actually join are then shipped.}
\ans{24}{1}{Multidatabase or federated systems give a global view over independent databases.}

\begin{question}{M}
Given below are two statements.\\
Statement I: In MapReduce, the number of reducers is set by the user or configuration.\\
Statement II: The number of map tasks always equals the number of reducers.
\optslong{Both Statement I and Statement II are true}{Both Statement I and Statement II are false}{Statement I is true but Statement II is false}{Statement I is false but Statement II is true}
\end{question}

\begin{answers}
\ans{1}{1}{Value is often added as a fifth V.}
\ans{2}{4}{Types of big data.}
\ans{3}{1}{The Secondary NameNode is not a hot standby for the NameNode.}
\ans{4}{2}{Hadoop 1 used 64 MB blocks.}
\ans{5}{2}{640 / 128 = 5 blocks, each stored 3 times: 3 $\times$ 640 = 1920 MB.}
\ans{6}{4}{One map task per input split, and by default one split per block: 1024 / 128 = 8.}
\ans{7}{2}{Map output is partitioned, sorted and sent to reducers, which write the final output.}
\ans{8}{1}{The default partitioner hashes the key modulo the number of reducers.}
\ans{9}{3}{The reducer sums the values for each word.}
\ans{10}{1}{YARN separates resource management from the MapReduce programming model.}
\ans{11}{3}{Other tools include Flume (log ingestion), ZooKeeper (coordination) and Oozie (workflow scheduling).}
\ans{12}{3}{Spark runs on clusters; it is faster because it keeps intermediate data in memory as RDDs.}
\ans{13}{2}{It is optimized for batch processing rather than interactive access.}
\ans{14}{3}{Blocks are replicated, by default three times.}
\ans{15}{3}{Data locality reduces network traffic.}
\ans{16}{2}{Other examples: DynamoDB (key-value), CouchDB (document), HBase (column-family).}
\ans{17}{3}{During a network partition a system must choose between consistency and availability.}
\ans{18}{3}{Many NoSQL systems relax consistency in favour of availability and scalability.}
\ans{19}{4}{With R = 2 and W = 2, read and write sets must overlap in at least one replica.}
\ans{20}{4}{2 + 2 > 3, so every read quorum overlaps every write quorum.}
\ans{21}{1}{It allows the database to scale out.}
\ans{22}{1}{Keys and nodes are mapped onto a ring; each key goes to the next node clockwise.}
\ans{23}{1}{MongoDB stores JSON-like BSON documents with a flexible schema.}
\ans{24}{1}{A field corresponds to a column.}
\ans{25}{3}{For example db.students.find(\{age: \{\$gt: 20\}\}).}
\ans{26}{3}{\$match filters documents, \$project reshapes them, and \$sort orders them.}
\ans{27}{2}{MongoDB also supports hashed indexes, used for hashed sharding.}
\ans{28}{2}{Queries are designed around the partition key.}
\ans{29}{4}{Cassandra is masterless (peer-to-peer); every node can accept reads and writes.}
\ans{30}{2}{Background compaction merges the SSTables.}
\ans{31}{3}{Schema design is driven by query access patterns.}
\ans{32}{2}{Others include Azure Cosmos DB and Google Cloud Bigtable/Firestore.}
\ans{33}{3}{Neo4j uses the Cypher query language over nodes and relationships.}
\ans{34}{3}{Reads may return stale data before the replicas converge.}
\ans{35}{3}{The Kappa architecture uses a single stream-processing layer.}
\ans{36}{2}{Hive, Sqoop and Oozie are batch-oriented tools.}
\ans{37}{3}{The Secondary NameNode only creates checkpoints; Hadoop 2 added NameNode high availability with a standby NameNode.}
\ans{38}{4}{Only the final reducer output is written to HDFS.}
\ans{39}{4}{A key-value store treats the value as opaque; access is by key.}
\ans{40}{1}{Flume ingests log data and Mahout provides machine-learning libraries.}
\ans{41}{4}{BSON is a binary representation of JSON.}
\ans{42}{4}{Queries that include the shard key can be routed to a single shard.}
\ans{43}{3}{The number of map tasks depends on the number of input splits, independently of the number of reducers.}
\end{answers}
